summary: MM-IssueLoc is a localization-only benchmark of 652 GitHub issue-PR pairs (608 repositories, 1,050 images) with file-level gold for every instance and function-level gold for 343. It pairs text-only, raw-image, and structured image-to-text inputs, and scores agents and retrievers with strict all-gold Acc@K. The headline that visual evidence is what current systems lack is not what the paired ablations show for the strongest agents.

claims.claim: The benchmark has 652 issue-PR instances, 23 languages, 7 image categories, 4 relevance levels, and both file- and function-level gold.
claims.evidence: Appendix C.1: 652 instances, 450 human and 202 AI-annotated, function view 343, difficulty 214/263/176, largest languages TypeScript 151 through PHP 20, '23 languages in total'. Tables 16-17 match the seven categories and the relevance counts (202/381/14/55). Section 3.4 instead says 24 languages. Figure 1 says 608 repositories.

claims.claim: Current systems are far from reliable multimodal localization: best agent 38.96 file Acc@5 and 22.45 function Acc@10; best retriever 33.86 function Acc@10.
claims.evidence: Table 2: OpenHands with GPT-5.2 is 38.96 File@5 and 22.45 Func@10; MM-IssueLoc-VL-Emb-8B is 33.86 Func@10 and only 32.82 File@5. The function-level winner is the authors' own retriever. Strict all-gold Acc@K is zero unless every gold location is inside K, so the 'far from reliable' reading is partly the metric. Single run, no CI.

claims.claim: Visual evidence provides a useful localization signal, but systems use it unevenly.
claims.evidence: Table 3: removing images costs the authors' 2B/8B retrievers 4.91 and 4.44 File@5, AgentLess with GPT-5.2 2.66, and OpenHands with GPT-5.2 only 0.31; OpenHands with Claude-Sonnet-4.6 is 0.92 better without images. Table 8: OpenHands File@5 is 36.14 on vital images and 34.55 on harmful ones. Table 13: multimodal training moves 8B File@5 only from 32.21 to 32.82, while Func@10 moves from 27.11 to 33.86.

claims.claim: Converting images to structured text (VCE) captures useful visual content, and raw pixels add little once that text exists.
claims.evidence: Table 4 file Acc@5: AgentLess Claude 25.15 to 28.53 with VCE (pixel residual +0.22); LocAgent Qwen3.5-122B 25.70 to 35.04 then 23.35 with pixels restored (residual -11.69); LocAgent GPT-5.2 falls from 19.13 to 16.12 with VCE alone. The residual is not stably near zero.

claims.claim: High localization scores on text-dominant SWE benchmarks do not transfer to multimodal issue localization.
claims.evidence: Table 15: OpenHands File@5 is 94.53 on SWE-bench-Lite and 90.20 on SWE-bench-Verified, versus 43.14 best File@5 on SWE-bench-MM. Those sets differ in language and difficulty, and gold there is derived from repair patches. On MM-IssueLoc itself, Table 3 shows the best agent's with-image and no-image File@5 differ by under one point, so the cross-benchmark drop is not identified as an image effect.

patterns.note: Issue localization is treated as repository exploration. OpenHands beats every retriever at file Acc@5 (38.96 vs 32.82), but the authors' embedding retriever beats every agent at function Acc@10 (33.86 vs 22.45). With the same Claude-Sonnet-4.6, OpenHands submits valid JSON on 98.6% of runs and scores 37.42 File@5, while Mini-SWE-Agent submits on 47.1% and scores 18.71 (App. A.2). Absolute strict accuracy stays low, and the best agent barely changes when images are removed.

A contrastive file-then-function curriculum on hard negatives raises 8B Func@10 from 20.70 (file-only stage) to 33.86 (Table 12), and image-conditioned training raises Func@10 from 27.11 to 33.86 (Table 13). The same image training barely moves File@5 (32.21 to 32.82). BM25 remains far behind (21.01 File@5, 19.83 Func@10). The winning retriever is trained on the authors' companion split of the same task.

New localization benchmark with paired image conditions, relevance labels, and a 55-instance harmful subset. The harmful images are mostly synthesized (natural rate under 1% in the human pool) and are a stress test, not a prevalence estimate.

OpenHands is described as a CodeAct agent with terminal, editor, and a finish action, capped at 10 iterations. It outperforms a bash-only Mini-SWE-Agent on the same model, but step limits, submission protocol, and tool surface all change together, so the interface is not isolated.

methodology.sample: 652 issue-PR instances, 1,050 images, 650 repository snapshots, 608 repositories; file gold on all 652, function gold on 343; 450 human-annotated and 202 AI-gated; 55 harmful-image instances, mostly synthesized; Java slice 44 instances.
methodology.baselines: BM25, bge-m3, SWERank small/large, Qwen3-VL-Embedding 2B/8B, plus AgentLess, LocAgent, OpenHands, and Mini-SWE-Agent. Cross-benchmark gold on SWE-bench Lite, Verified, and Multimodal is derived from repair patches.
methodology.models: Agent backends include GPT-5.2, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Kimi-K2.5, Gemini-3-Pro, and Qwen3.5-122B. Retrievers include the authors' MM-IssueLoc-VL-Embedding 2B/8B initialized from Qwen3-VL-Embedding.
methodology.variance: No confidence intervals or repeated agent runs. Training uses one seed per stage (42 then 43).
methodology.ablations: Image on/off (Table 3), VCE vs VCE+image (Table 4), curriculum stage and text-only training (Tables 12-13), relevance/category/language/annotation slices (App. B.1), external image ablation on SWE-bench-MM (Table 14).
methodology.contamination_controls: Training rows are disjoint from the benchmark at instance_id. No check that frontier models had already seen the public issues or PRs. AI labels come from a VLM gate whose models are not named.
methodology.languages: 23 languages in Appendix C.1 (24 stated once in §3.4), including TypeScript, Python, JavaScript, C++, Java, Go, C#, Rust, C, and PHP. Function labels depend on tree-sitter and are missing for some languages.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint only (v1, 16 Jul 2026); comment and journal_ref empty.
standards.artifacts: Benchmark repository claimed at github.com/Jasaxion/MM-IssueLoc-Bench. Prompts are in Appendices D-E; training hyperparameters and hardware are in Appendix A. Per-instance predictions are said to be released. Repository contents were not inspected.

biases.detail: Every Acc@K cell is a single run. Training reports a seed but not repeated trials.

Strict all-gold Acc@K treats a partial but useful file list as a total miss, and gold is the human PR diff rather than a minimal causal set. The paper states both limits and still uses the metric for the 'not reliable' headline.
The best function Acc@10 (33.86) is the authors' retriever, trained on a companion split built with the same pipeline and scored on their own benchmark.
Instances are public GitHub issues. Frontier agents may have seen the issue text or the merged PR. The 202 AI-annotated rows are admitted by unnamed VLMs.
Image-training gains are largest on the authors' function metric; the same 8B model does not benefit from images on SWE-bench-MM (Table 14: no-image File@5 29.41, with-image 28.43).
Agent iteration caps are given, but token counts and dollar cost are not, so the agent-versus-retriever gap is not cost-adjusted.
The abstract attributes the SWE-bench gap to multimodal evidence. Table 3 shows the strongest agent is almost indifferent to whether the image is present.

coi.affiliations: Tsinghua University and JD.com. Several authors list JD.com email addresses; the corresponding author is at Tsinghua.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Open-weight and commercial models (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Kimi, Qwen) and public agent frameworks. No JD product is scored.
coi.detail: Company affiliation is real, but the evaluated systems are not that company's products. The favorable function-level number is their research retriever on their benchmark, which is self-evaluation rather than a vendor grading its own product.

verdict_reason: The benchmark construction and the paired image ablations are usable: 652 real issue-PR instances, several agent and retriever families, and within-benchmark image removal. The abstract's transfer story is not identified. Text SWE-bench File@5 near 90 versus multimodal File@5 near 40 compares different languages and repos, and on this benchmark the best agent moves by less than one File@5 point when images are removed. Relevance labels are non-monotonic, harmful images are mostly synthetic, 202 of 652 rows are model-annotated, gold is the PR diff, and no run is repeated. The best function score is the authors' own retriever.
applicability: Useful as a caution for issue and bug localization in the multi-repo Java backend, not as a reason to add a screenshot channel. The Java slice is 44 instances and OpenHands file Acc@5 there is 39.53, almost the same as the overall 38.96, so Java is not a special failure. UI screenshots, the largest image category (177), are a poor match for the services; logs and error text are the closer analogue, and VCE's mixed results say a fixed image-to-text dump is not a reliable substitute for reading the issue. For the harness: do not treat a high SWE-bench localization score as evidence the agent can find the right files once an issue carries images, and do not expect raw images to move file selection for a strong tool-using agent. Strict all-gold accuracy will look harsh on multi-module cross-repository changes that touch several repositories. A retriever can rank functions once candidates are enumerated, but the winning model was trained for this benchmark.

conflicts_with.detail: That review's surviving result is that exploration agents beat embedding RAG on repository question answering (about 4 to 12 points, at roughly 13x the tokens). Here the ranking flips at function granularity: the trained multimodal retriever's Func@10 (33.86) beats the best agent's (22.45), while agents still lead at file Acc@5. The tasks differ (free-form QA versus strict all-gold localization), but a harness should not treat 'agents beat retrieval' as settled for bug localization.
